property_summary: For any caller, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored contract owner (the address set at construction), whereas the mutant returns the caller (msg.sender) for some callers — so owner() must equal the originally stored owner for all callers, a property the bug violates for some input caller address.

For every caller address, the correct contract's owner() returns the immutable constructor-set owner; the mutant returns msg.sender for some callers, so for those callers owner() will differ from the stored owner.

For every caller address, the reference contract's owner() returns the fixed owner set at construction; the mutant returns msg.sender for some callers, so there exists a caller for which owner() != stored owner.

For every caller address, the reference contract's owner() view always returns the single fixed owner address set at construction; the mutant instead returns the caller (msg.sender) for some callers, so there exists a caller for which owner() != the stored constructor owner.

For every caller address, the correct contract's owner() returns the fixed owner set at construction; the mutant returns msg.sender for some caller, so there exists a caller for which owner() != the stored constructor owner.

For any non-zero newOwner address, transferOwnership(newOwner) called by the current owner always succeeds and sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant removes the non-zero check and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed (setting owner to zero) which violates the intended rule that owner can never be set to the zero address.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner must never allow owner() to become address(0); the mutant removes the require check and therefore for newOwner = address(0) the mutant permits owner() == address(0) while the reference never does.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must never result in owner() == address(0); the mutant removes the require check and thus allows owner() to become address(0) when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must never result in owner() == address(0); the buggy mutant allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to set owner to zero while the reference prevents this.

For any caller that's the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must never result in owner() == address(0); the mutant removes the require check and so allows owner() to become address(0) for newOwner == address(0).

For any address input _operator, calling setOperator(_operator) by the owner sets c.operator() equal to the provided _operator; the mutant instead sets operator to address(0) for some inputs, so this equality can be violated.

For every input address x, when the owner calls setOperator(x) the contract's operator getter returns exactly x; the mutant instead sets operator to address(0) for some inputs, violating this equality.

For every address newOperator, when the owner calls setOperator(newOperator) the contract's operator() getter equals newOperator; the mutant that always assigns address(0) will violate this for any newOperator != address(0).
For any address X passed to setOperator by the owner, after the call c.operator() equals X (reference); the mutant that always assigns address(0) will make c.operator() != X for any X != address(0).

For any address newOp passed by the owner to setOperator, the reference contract sets operator() to newOp; the mutant breaks this by setting operator() to address(0) for some inputs (any newOp != address(0)).

Calling setOperator(x) by the owner must set operator() to the provided argument x; the mutant instead sets operator() to the caller, violating this when the owner calls setOperator with any x != owner.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(address x) makes c.operator() equal to the provided argument x; the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender so for some x (x != owner) this property is violated.

For any address x and for any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(x) results in c.operator() == x in the reference; the mutant sets operator to the caller instead, so when x != owner the mutant violates this rule.

For any address newOp and when called by the contract owner, setOperator(newOp) makes c.operator() equal the provided newOp; the mutant instead sets operator to the caller (owner), so when newOp != owner the mutant will violate this property.

For any address newOperator and when the owner calls setOperator(newOperator), the contract's operator() equals the provided newOperator; the mutant instead assigns operator to the caller (owner), so when newOperator != owner the mutant violates this rule.

For every input address x passed to setOperator(x) by the owner, the contract's operator becomes x (reference) — the mutant instead sets operator() to owner(), so there exists some x (x != owner()) that makes the mutant's operator differ from the provided x.

For any address newOp passed to setOperator by the owner, the contract's operator becomes exactly newOp (reference); the mutant instead sets operator to owner(), so when newOp != owner() the mutant violates this.

For every address candidate 'newOperator' passed by the owner to setOperator, the reference contract sets operator() to that exact address; the mutant instead always sets operator() to owner(), so when newOperator != owner() the mutant will differ and break this rule.

For every address newOp passed to setOperator by the owner, the contract's operator() becomes equal to the provided newOp; the mutant always sets operator() to owner() so it will violate this rule whenever newOp != owner().

For any address newOperator supplied by the owner to setOperator, the reference contract sets operator() to exactly newOperator; the mutant instead sets operator() to owner(), so when newOperator != owner() the mutant will violate this property.

Owner-only functions can be successfully called when tx.origin == owner (any caller) under the reference contract, but the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin allows calls only when the externally owned account origin matches owner, breaking calls made via a contract caller for some caller addresses.

Any call to owner-only function setOperator(msg.sender) initiated with msg.sender == owner should succeed irrespective of whether the caller is a contract or EOA; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin wrongly blocks calls made through contract callers (where tx.origin != owner), so for some contract callers the mutant will fail while the reference always allows them.

For all callers X (EOA or contract) invoking setOperator via a tx.origin = any EOA owner, the reference contract allows the owner (owner() == msg.sender) to call setOperator when msg.sender equals owner, but the mutant blocks calls when the call is relayed through a contract (tx.origin != owner); thus the reference always permits a contract caller that was set as owner to call setOperator, while the mutant sometimes rejects such relayed calls.

For any caller contract Ctr that is itself set as owner of the contract under test, calling setOperator through that contract (so msg.sender == owner() inside C) always succeeds on the reference implementation, but the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin will sometimes reject such calls when tx.origin != owner(), causing operator to not be updated.

For all callers (EOAs or contracts) that are the contract owner (owner() == msg.sender), calling setOperator(...) always sets operator to the provided address in the reference; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin can block owner calls relayed through a contract (tx.origin != owner), so for some contract callers the mutant will not update operator.

For all callers (any fuzzed caller address), when setOperator(...) is invoked by the contract owner the operator state is updated to the provided address; the mutant that makes onlyOwner a no-op allows non-owner callers to also change operator, so there exists a caller address for which calling setOperator succeeds on the mutant but should be disallowed on the reference.

Under the reference contract only the owner can successfully call setOperator(address) so operator can only be changed when the caller is owner; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check allowing a non-owner caller to change operator, so there exists a caller address and param where operator differs between reference and mutant.

For all callers and newOperator addresses, only the contract owner can change c.operator() via setOperator; the mutant makes onlyOwner a no-op so some non-owner caller can change operator, violating this rule.

For every caller and candidate operator address, only the contract owner may cause c.operator() to change via setOperator; the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction so some non-owner caller can change operator, producing a differing operator value.

Only the contract owner can cause operator to change via setOperator(address); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so a non-owner caller can change operator, making operator differ when called by a non-owner.

For any input address X passed to setRewardsRecipient by the owner, the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == X afterwards; the mutant instead clears it to address(0) for some X, so there exists inputs where the stored value differs.

For any address input provided by the owner to setRewardsRecipient, the correct contract stores that exact address in rewardsRecipient; the mutant clears rewardsRecipient to address(0) instead, so there exist inputs (any non-zero address) where the stored value differs.

For any address provided by the owner to setRewardsRecipient, the correct contract sets rewardsRecipient to that exact address; the mutant instead sometimes stores address(0) (so there exist inputs where rewardsRecipient differs).

For every address x passed by the owner to setRewardsRecipient(x), the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == x afterwards; the mutant instead always stores address(0) so there exist inputs (any non-zero address) where rewardsRecipient differs.

For any address provided by the contract owner to setRewardsRecipient, the reference contract stores that exact address in rewardsRecipient; the mutant instead clears rewardsRecipient to address(0) so there exist owner-provided inputs where the stored rewardsRecipient differs.

For any caller passed as _recipeint to setRewardsRecipient by the owner, the contract stores the provided _recipeint as rewardsRecipient; the mutant that stores msg.sender instead will cause rewardsRecipient != _recipeint for some inputs (when owner != _recipeint).

After the owner calls setRewardsRecipient(x), the contract's rewardsRecipient equals the provided address x for all inputs; the mutant that stores msg.sender instead will break this whenever the owner is not equal to x.

For any address X provided by the owner to setRewardsRecipient, the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == X; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will violate this property whenever owner != X (i.e., some fuzzed X will differ).

When the owner calls setRewardsRecipient(addr), the contract's rewardsRecipient is set to the provided addr for every input; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will violate this whenever the provided addr differs from the owner (so some fuzzed addr will make the mutant disagree).

When the owner calls setRewardsRecipient(x), the contract's rewardsRecipient must equal the provided x for every input; the mutant that stores msg.sender instead will violate this whenever the provided x differs from the owner.

For any input address X, calling setRewardsRecipient(X) sets rewardsRecipient to X; the mutant instead sets rewardsRecipient to the current operator, so for some X (when X != operator) the mutant will differ.
For any input address r, calling setRewardsRecipient(r) sets C.rewardsRecipient() == r in the reference; the mutant instead always sets it to operator, so when r != operator the mutant violates this.

For any address r passed to setRewardsRecipient(r), the correct contract sets rewardsRecipient == r; the mutant instead sets rewardsRecipient == operator, so when r != operator the mutant will differ.

For every address input r, calling setRewardsRecipient(r) on the correct contract results in rewardsRecipient() == r (it stores the passed-in recipient); the mutant instead ignores the input and stores operator, so for some r != operator the mutant violates this.

For any address r passed to setRewardsRecipient(r), the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == r (it records the provided recipient); the mutant ignores the input and stores operator instead, so when r != operator the mutant will violate this property.

For any address X passed to setRewardsRecipient, the reference contract sets rewardsRecipient == X (and emits the event); the mutant emits the event but does not update state so rewardsRecipient != X for some inputs, thus violating the rule.

For any address input, calling setRewardsRecipient(addr) causes the contract's rewardsRecipient getter to equal addr in the reference; the mutant does not update state so for some addr the getter will differ.

For any address x, calling setRewardsRecipient(x) on the correct contract sets rewardsRecipient == x (and thus the getter returns x); the mutant emits the event but does not store the value, so for some x the getter will differ and the property will be violated.

For every address a, after calling setRewardsRecipient(a) the correct contract's rewardsRecipient getter equals a; the mutant fails to update the state so for some fuzzed addresses the getter will differ.

For every address a, calling setRewardsRecipient(a) on the correct contract results in c.rewardsRecipient() == a; the mutant that omits the assignment will make c.rewardsRecipient() != a for some fuzzed addresses, so the property distinguishes them.

For any input address x, calling setRewardsRecipient(x) on the correct contract always sets rewardsRecipient to x (i.e. rewardsRecipient equals the provided address after the call); the mutant ignores non-zero inputs and thus for some x (any non-zero) the stored rewardsRecipient will differ.
